tek_cumle: A film does not give us the story; it gives us the plot, and we build the story ourselves — every concept this week describes how that building work is guided.

bolumler.html:
This week we worked through Bordwell and Thompson’s chapter on narrative in five steps. First we set up the basic distinction: the story (fabula) is the whole that the viewer builds, chronologically and causally, out of the events that are shown and implied; the plot (syuzhet) is everything the film concretely presents to us on screen and on the soundtrack. Next we looked at causality: in classical narrative, the engine that links events together is mostly the characters’ desires and goals. On the third day we split time into three axes: order, duration and frequency. On the last two days we discussed two settings of narration: range — how much information we have access to; and depth — how far we enter a character’s inner world.

Remember: the concept of diegesis (the story world) rests on this distinction. Anything whose source lies within the story world is diegetic; elements that belong only to the plot, such as the credits or film music the characters cannot hear, are nondiegetic.

quiz.soru: Which option best defines the story (fabula)?
secenekler: The events shown directly on screen and the order in which they are shown
The whole that the viewer builds, chronologically and causally, from the events shown and implied
All of the film’s material, including the music and credits
The director’s script plan before shooting
quiz.aciklama: The story is the whole the viewer builds; it also includes events that are not on screen but that we infer.

quiz.soru: Which of the following belongs to the plot (syuzhet) but not to the story (fabula)?
secenekler: An event in the character’s past that is never shown
Film music laid over the scene that the characters do not hear
Three days that we infer have passed between two scenes
The goal the character announces at the start of the film
quiz.aciklama: Music the characters cannot hear does not belong to the story world; it is part of the plot only.

quiz.soru: In classical narrative cinema, what is usually the main causal engine linking events together?
secenekler: The characters’ desires and goals, and the obstacles in their way
Chance and coincidence
Natural cycles (the seasons, night and day)
Camera movement and editing rhythm
quiz.aciklama: In classical narrative, causality mostly springs from the characters’ desires and goals; coincidence is secondary.

quiz.soru: Which temporal technique are the color sections of Memento based on?
secenekler: Frequency: showing the same event over and over in exactly the same way
Duration: stretching every scene out in slow motion
Order: arranging the sections in reverse of the story’s chronology
Crosscutting: showing two places simultaneously
quiz.aciklama: The color sections are arranged in reverse chronological order; like Leonard, the viewer begins each scene without knowing what came before.

quiz.soru: We watch twenty years of a character’s life in a two-minute montage sequence. This is an example of which relationship between screen duration and story duration?
secenekler: Expansion
Equal duration / real time
Reverse order
Compression
quiz.aciklama: Screen duration is much shorter than story duration: compression.

quiz.soru: In Rashomon, the fact that we watch four separate versions of the incident in the forest relates primarily to what, on the axis of time?
secenekler: Frequency: a single story event presented more than once in the plot
Duration: the event shown in real time
Order: events given in reverse chronology
Depth: a shift to fully objective narration
quiz.aciklama: A single event is presented four times in the plot; this is a matter of frequency (and the fact that the versions differ also calls reliability into question).

quiz.soru: Which statement is true of restricted narration?
secenekler: The viewer always knows more than all the characters
Our knowledge is largely limited to what a single character (or a small group) knows
The film takes place in a single location
The film has no dialogue
quiz.aciklama: In restricted narration, our knowledge is limited to what a character knows; option A describes unrestricted narration.

quiz.soru: The camera uses a point-of-view shot to show that we are looking through a character’s eyes. In terms of depth of narration, what is this?
secenekler: Objective narration
Perceptual subjectivity
Mental subjectivity
Unrestricted range
quiz.aciklama: Seeing what the character sees is perceptual subjectivity; an inner voice, a memory or a fantasy would be mental subjectivity.

quiz.soru: Which of the following is a nondiegetic element?
secenekler: A song playing on the radio in the character’s car
Two characters talking to each other
Suspense music with no source in the story world, which the characters do not hear
The sound of a door slamming in the scene
quiz.aciklama: Music whose source is not in the story world is nondiegetic; the radio, the conversation and the door are diegetic.

quiz.soru: In the courtroom scenes of Rashomon, the witnesses speak directly to the camera; the official questioning them is neither seen nor heard. What is the most important narrative effect of this choice?
secenekler: It puts the viewer in the questioner’s place; it is up to us to decide which account to believe
It turns the film into a documentary
It switches to unrestricted narration and reveals the truth definitively
It adds a nondiegetic narrator to the film
quiz.aciklama: The viewer takes the place of the unseen questioner; the film gives no definitive verdict and leaves the decision to us.

sorular: Explain the difference between story and plot with an example.
What do restricted and unrestricted narration mean?
What do diegetic and nondiegetic elements mean?
analiz:
Answer each short-answer question in 3–6 sentences, in your own words, with at least one film example.

Assignment: Compare the four accounts in Rashomon in terms of range of narration and reliability.

Length: 600–900 words.

Roadmap (try to answer these):

  • Whose knowledge is each of the four accounts (the bandit, the wife, the dead samurai, the woodcutter) based on? What can each narrator know, and what can’t they know? How does this limit the range of each section?
  • When the film stacks these four restricted accounts on top of one another, do we arrive at broader knowledge overall, or at greater uncertainty?
  • Reliability: look at the light in which each narrator presents themselves. What interests (honor, shame, guilt) shape each account?
  • How does the frame narrative (the three men talking at the gate in the rain) organize the narration? Does the claim that the last narrator is a “neutral witness” hold up?
  • Use at least two more of this week’s concepts: story/plot, frequency, or depth (subjective/objective).
  • Support your claims with concrete scenes: describe at least two scenes by looking at what is happening in the camerawork or the sound.

What I’ll look for when assessing: that you use the concepts correctly (especially that you don’t confuse range with depth), that you support your claims with scenes, and that rather than getting stuck on the question “which version is true?” you analyze how the film constructs that question.
gozlem: In any TV episode or video you watch today, pick a single moment and ask: right now, do I know more than the characters, less, or the same? Note the answer in one sentence.

terimler.tanim: The whole set of events the viewer builds, chronologically and causally, from the events shown and implied.
Everything the film concretely presents to us, including nondiegetic elements.
How many times a story event is presented in the plot.
How broadly the viewer has access to story information: from restricted to unrestricted.
How far the narration enters a character’s perceptual and mental world: from objective to subjective.
Whether or not an element’s source lies within the story world.

yarin: Week 3, Day 1: we move from narrative to the image itself — mise-en-scène: setting, costume, lighting and the placement of actors.
